title: Contemporary Indian Art
summary: Contemporary art began with the British rule after the decline of the Mughal empire. Raja Ravi Varma, Abanindranath Tagore, Amrita Shergil, Rabindranath Tagore and Jamini Roy were pioneers. These artists were exposed to German Expressionism, Cubism, Fauvism, Dadaism and Surrealism but struggled to retain Indian identity; a combination of western technique and Indian spiritualism became the essence of Indian art, and they also tried far-eastern methods. Many experiments were done with print making (woodcut, lithograph, etching). Pradosh Das Gupta, Prankrishna Pal, Nirode Mazumder, Paritosh Sen and others of the Calcutta Group held their first show in 1943; the Progressive Artists Group of Bombay exhibited the paintings of F.N. Souza, Raza, M.F. Hussain, K.H. Ara and others in 1947. Benode Behari Mukherjee, Ramkinkar Vaij and Sailoz Mukherjee inclined to Japanese and folk art. Devi Prosad Roy Chowdhury and Saroda Ukil of the Bengal School introduced the modern art movement in the north and south of India; K.C.S. Panikar and Srinivasalu were students of Roy Chowdhury, and Saroda Ukil founded an art school in Delhi. Some painters settled abroad and became internationally successful.

Artist: Krishna Reddy (student of Kala Bhavan, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan). Period: 1962. Size: 37.5 x 49.5 cm. Medium: intaglio on paper. Print making (graphics) is a popular art form used by western artists for centuries; Indian painters took interest from the end of the 19th century; techniques include etching, dry point, aquatint, intaglio, lithography and oleography; the main advantage is that many copies of the same work can be produced (Raja Ravi Varma popularised his paintings through oleographs). Intaglio is the reverse of the relief method: the lines of the design are incised in a copper or zinc plate, ink is held in the engraved furrows, the surface is wiped clean with a scraper, damp paper is laid on it and a print is taken under pressure in a machine. In 'Whirlpool' Reddy creates new forms from known objects and takes the form into abstraction; his interest is to capture the force of nature – everything is lost in the cosmic whirlpool; the images (stars, flowers, clouds) are non-representational; his early experience in sculpture helps the relief-type intaglio effects.

Artist: Benode Behari Mukherjee (1904–80), a student of Nandalal Bose. Period: 1947. Medium: Fresco Buono. Place: mural on the wall of Hindi Bhavan, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan. He loved nature, learnt landscaping from Japan and used simple, rational lines like Japanese artists with a calligraphic quality. He had weak eyesight from childhood and became totally blind later, but his creative urge did not stop: despite blindness he created a huge mural at Kala Bhavan. Fresco Buono is wall painting in which powdered pigments mixed in water are applied to freshly laid wet lime plaster so that the colour becomes part of the wall and lasts long. The mural depicts saints of different religions of India; the composition suits the size of the walls; huge, elongated figures are arranged in river-like flowing movement in harmony and rhythm, with a monument-like quality like sculptures on Gothic church walls; the emphatic verticality is balanced by smaller figures in horizontal continuity – the large figures show spiritual greatness and the smaller ones the common people in everyday activities. Lines are emphatic and colours limited: brown, yellow ochre and terraverte.

Artist: K.C.S. Panikar (1911–77). Medium: oil on board. Size: 43 x 124 cm. Date: 1965. He was the most influential pioneer of the contemporary art movement in South India, a student of D.P. Roy Chowdhury at the Madras School of Art; he did odd jobs as a telegraph operator and insurance agent before establishing himself; his style moved from realistic to geometric; as a great teacher he founded the first artists' village of India, 'Cholamandalam', near Chennai. 'Words and Symbols' is from his series 'Words' and 'Symbols': an experimental work in which space is covered with calligraphy, using mathematical symbols, Arabic figures, Roman and Malayalam scripts to make a design that looks like a horoscope, with Tantric symbolic diagrams; colour plays a nominal role.

Artist: Francis Newton Souza (1924–2002). Period: 1961. Size: 78.7 x 132.1 cm. Medium: oil. Collection: Jahangir Nicholson Museum. He was born in Goa, grew up in Mumbai, was expelled from school and again from the J.J. School of Art in 1945, and was one of the founders of the Progressive Artists Group (1947); he later settled in London (also lived in New York) and became one of the top five artists to represent India internationally. He protested against religious and social superstition, was inspired by Post-Impressionists and German Expressionists, was greatly influenced by Picasso and Matisse and combined Indian temple sculpture forms with western art. 'Landscape in Red' is an experimental cityscape showing a city as a concrete jungle with a mysterious character; calligraphic lines are arranged with colours; red dominates with splashes of green; no rule of perspective is followed, yet the depth of space is clearly defined.

vsa: What do you know about the 'Progressive Artists Group'? Name a few artists of this group.

The Progressive Artists Group of Bombay was formed in 1947 and exhibited its paintings that year; its artists included F.N. Souza, S.H. Raza, M.F. Hussain and K.H. Ara. They took western influences while searching for an Indian identity.

F.N. Souza's 'Landscape in Red' (oil, 1961) is an experimental cityscape showing a city as a concrete jungle with a mysterious character. Calligraphic lines are arranged with colours; red predominates with a few splashes of green; no rule of perspective is followed yet depth of space is clearly shown.
Write a note on Francis Newton Souza.

Souza (1924–2002) was born in Goa and grew up in Mumbai; expelled from J.J. School of Art in 1945, he was a founder of the Progressive Artists Group in 1947 and later settled in London. He protested against superstitions, was influenced by Picasso and Matisse, combined Indian temple sculpture with western art and is compared with Picasso.
What do you know about the Indian painter who became blind?

Benode Behari Mukherjee, a student of Nandalal Bose, had weak eyesight from childhood and became totally blind later but still created a huge mural at Kala Bhavan, Santiniketan, including 'The Mediaeval Saints' in Fresco Buono at Hindi Bhavan.

Graphics or print making is an art form in which a number of copies of the same picture are produced. Techniques include etching, dry point, aquatint, intaglio, lithography and oleography.

State the methods and techniques used by contemporary artists of India.

They combined western techniques with Indian spiritualism, used far-eastern (Japanese and Chinese) methods, and experimented a great deal with print making (woodcut, lithograph, etching, intaglio) and with folk art and murals.
sa: Describe the technique and message of Krishna Reddy's 'Whirlpool'.

'Whirlpool' (1962, intaglio on paper) is made by incising the design lines in a copper or zinc plate; ink is held only in the furrows, the surface is wiped clean, damp paper is laid on it and the print is taken under pressure. Reddy creates abstract forms from stars, flowers and clouds to capture the force of nature: everything is lost in the cosmic whirlpool. His early training in sculpture gives the relief-like intaglio effect.

Painted by Benode Behari Mukherjee in 1947 on the wall of Hindi Bhavan, Visva-Bharati, in Fresco Buono, it shows saints of different religions as huge elongated figures arranged in flowing, river-like movement with a monument-like quality like Gothic sculpture; the emphatic verticality is balanced by smaller figures in horizontal continuity showing common people. The lines are emphatic and the colours limited to brown, yellow ochre and terraverte.
Write about two painters of India who settled abroad and became famous.

F.N. Souza settled in London and also lived in New York; he became one of the top five artists to represent India internationally, with works like 'Landscape in Red'. Krishna Reddy, a Santiniketan-trained print maker, became famous for intaglio prints like 'Whirlpool'.

la: Describe the influences that helped in the development of contemporary art of India.

Contemporary art began with British rule. Indian artists were exposed to German Expressionism, Cubism, Fauvism, Dadaism and Surrealism, yet struggled to keep their Indian identity; a combination of western technique and Indian spirituality became its essence. They also used far-eastern methods, experimented with print making (woodcut, lithography, etching), folk art and Japanese art, and groups such as the Calcutta Group (1943) and the Progressive Artists Group (1947) formed. Teachers like Roy Chowdhury, Saroda Ukil and Panikar spread the movement in the north and south; some artists settled abroad.
Describe in brief one famous painting of Panikar or Souza.

K.C.S. Panikar's 'Words and Symbols' (1965, oil on board) covers space with calligraphy of mathematical symbols, Arabic figures, Roman and Malayalam scripts and Tantric diagrams that look like a horoscope; colour plays a nominal role. F.N. Souza's 'Landscape in Red' (1961, oil) is an experimental cityscape of a concrete jungle with red predominating and splashes of green; calligraphic lines are used and no perspective is followed, yet depth of space is clear.
Write a note on Benode Behari Mukherjee and his mural 'The Mediaeval Saints'.

Benode Behari Mukherjee (1904–80), a student of Nandalal Bose, loved nature, learnt landscape from Japan and used simple calligraphic lines. Weak-eyed since childhood and finally blind, he still created a huge mural at Kala Bhavan. 'The Mediaeval Saints' (1947) on the wall of Hindi Bhavan, Visva-Bharati, is a Fresco Buono wall painting of saints of different religions as huge elongated figures in flowing rhythm, balanced by smaller figures of common people, in brown, yellow ochre and terraverte.
